source.quote: Problem Definition: This study examines a seller’s joint information disclosure and pricing decisions when launching a new product with an easy-to-communicate objective attribute and a hard-to-describe subjective attribute.
We analyze how consumer search cost, inventory level, and channel structure shape the seller’s optimal information strategy.

The rationale is that a larger search cost or limited product availability incentivizes the firm to disclose information in order to attract poten­ tially high-valuation consumers to engage in search.
In our base model, we assume that the product is exclusively sold through offline stores.
In practice, firms are typically restricted, or at the very least influenced, by their limited inventory levels, which can stem from, for example, nonnegligible procure­ ment and holding costs.
Interestingly, when the inventory level is high, the seller conceals information to retain the “diamond-in-the-rough” consumers, aiming to match the abundant inventory with high demand.
Thus, consumers must invest the search cost c and have learned their total valuations before purchases.

conditions: When a consumer observes a realized signal S = s, she updates her posterior belief of X using the Bayesian rule.
First, although signal realizations S = s may differ across consumers, this does not mean that the seller sends individualized messages.

Specifically, it induces a stochastic order on the distributions of the posterior mean E[X|S], known as the rotation order (Johnson and Myatt 2006, Guo 2023), and the signal S becomes more precise as q ∈[0,1] increases (Shaked 2007).
